title: Lightweight context propagator and SDK bridge for high-throughput inference
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Problem: Our hosted inference path and Dedicated runtime see a significant fraction of short-lived, high-frequency requests where standard SDK context propagation (rich JSON headers, synchronous hooks) adds measurable tail-latency and CPU overhead. Several SDK integrations (node/python/go) instrument at request entry and end but duplicate work and pay serialization costs even when tracing is sampled-out.

Goals: 1) Provide a minimal, cross-language propagation envelope that reduces per-request CPU and allocation overhead for the happy path. 2) Make it easy for language SDKs and middleware to adopt with a single cohesive bridge implementation so rollout is consistent. 3) Preserve trace fidelity for sampled requests and graceful degradation for unsampled or partially instrumented clients. 4) Support HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSocket transports without bespoke header formats per-transport.

Constraints and trade-offs: - Must be safe for high-traffic inference routes (millions of qps across customers) and add <0.5ms median per-request overhead. - Backwards compatible with existing OpenTelemetry-compatible headers where possible; avoid breaking managed partners. - Avoid heavy runtime dependencies in SDKs (no mandatory OTLP exporters). - Keep on-wire footprint minimal to limit additional bandwidth on small prompt requests.

Proposal: Implement a two-part solution: 1) Binary compact propagator: a tiny binary header (Base64 over existing header key) carrying LTT: trace-id (64 bits), span-id (64 bits), flags (sampling, priority), lightweight baggage fingerprint (32 bits) and an optional 8-byte request sequence token for KV-cache affinity. This header is designed to be parsed with a single memcopy and bitmasks. 2) SDK bridge library: provide a thin, zero-allocation bridge for Node/Python/Go that (a) exposes a single entrypoint for extracting/injecting the compact header, (b) provides a lazy-attach hook that only allocates full span objects when sampling = true or when an SDK-level observer requests full spans, and (c) offers an async-safe fallback for websocket frame reassembly.

Design notes: - Sampling reconciliation: servers accept both the compact header and classic W3C Traceparent; when both present, use server-side sampling policy and emit a reconciliation event for later analysis. - Backfill strategy: clients that cannot produce compact headers will continue to send traceparent; we will auto-translate server-side and emit the compact envelope for internal downstream calls. - Rollout: feature-gate by SDK version and runtime config; enable lightweight mode per-route in Console.

Open questions: - Should the compact header include a 16-bit checksum? (pros: detect corruption; cons: increase parse cost) - How to handle 3rd-party proxies that rewrite Base64 headers? - Metrics to track adoption and regressions: per-route median overhead, percent of requests with compact header, sampling reconciliation rate, error delta for traced vs untraced flows.
acceptance_criteria: Server accepts and parses compact header for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC with <0.5ms median added latency on benchmark harness (noise-corrected)
SDK bridge libraries implemented for Node/Python/Go with lazy allocation path documented; unit tests covering injection/extraction and sampling=false fast-path
End-to-end test showing that sampled traces contain full span lifecycles and unsampled requests avoid allocation (heap/alloc metrics measured)
Console rollout toggle deployable per-route and host; telemetry showing percent of requests using compact header within first week
Graceful fallback implemented: when compact header corrupt or missing, server-side translator maps existing traceparent without breaking flow
